title: Why Candidate Experience Matters in Hiring (August 2026)
summary: Explore why candidate experience matters for attracting top talent and building a stronger hiring process in October 2026.
body_markdown:
Candidates form a view of your company long before an offer is on the table, and that view shapes whether they accept, recommend the role to others, or apply again for a future opening. Most hiring teams manage[candidate experience](https://www.dover.com/) reactively, fixing it only after an offer is declined or a poor review appears online. This guide covers why candidate experience matters for hiring outcomes and three changes that make a process feel more organized and personal.


**TLDR:**


-


Bad candidate experience causes 63% of job seekers to reject offers, and 27% will actively discourage others from applying.


-


Rejected candidates are 80% more likely to reapply if your process treated them well, expanding your future hiring pool.


-


Personalized outreach can increase candidate interest; generic communication cuts your pipeline before it starts.


-


In 2026, 61% of job seekers report being ghosted after interviews, and only 26% say they’ve had a great experience overall.


-


Speed, preparation at each stage, and clear rejection messages are the three areas where most hiring processes lose candidates.


## What Is Candidate Experience?


Candidate experience is defined as: **the impression candidates have of your company after going through your hiring process.**


Think of all of the things that you, as a job seeker, would expect from a company. That list would likely include:


-


Clear guidelines on the interview process, and key contacts


-


The ability to find information about the culture and benefits


-


Speed and smooth handling in scheduling


-


Opportunities to provide feedback


-


The general demeanor of interviewers, including timeliness, professionalism, and active listening


## 3 Reasons Why Candidate Experience Matters


### 1. It’s Critical to Employer Brand and Company Perception.


With tech unemployment rates at historically low levels, more candidates are doing their research, including reading employee reviews and interview experiences on sites like Glassdoor and Comparably.


Negative experiences can hurt your online reputation a great deal, as nearly[37% of candidates](https://www.careerplug.com/blog/candidate-experience-statistics/) said they’ve left a negative review online after having a poor experience.


However, positive experiences go a long way and nearly double the rewards:[61% of candidates](https://www.careerplug.com/blog/candidate-experience-statistics/) said they’ve left a positive review online after having a positive experience.


### 2. It Increases Your Pool of Potential Candidates.


Candidate experience isn’t only effective with people you hire. **Job applicants who do not receive a job offer are 80% more likely to apply again if they already had a positive candidate experience.**


By making a good impression, you’ll have a larger pool of future candidates to pull from for potential openings that they may be a better fit for.


### 3. It Can Help You Outcompete Other Offers.


If a candidate is presented with two similar offers (including salary), the deciding factor will undoubtedly be the experience they had interviewing with your team, which is why knowing how to[beat competing offers](https://www.dover.com/blog/beat-competing-offers-startup-hiring) starts well before the final round. In fact, **the interview process is often the only direct signal candidates have about what it would actually be like to work there** .


It makes sense: your hiring process is the only example they have to gauge your culture and their future colleagues.


Candidate experience also begins before anyone is screened. It starts with your initial touchpoint to candidates. We’ve seen the effect it has on attracting passive talent to apply, as[personalized emails](https://www.dover.com/blog/how-to-write-great-recruiting-emails) **can increase candidate interest.**


“Personalized emails have been a game-changer for us in breaking through the noise to stand out. We’ve seen a lot of responses that say: ‘Hey, I get a lot of these, but I had to respond because you took the time to really look at my background.’”


**Ray Lyons, VP of Product at eSpark Learning**


## 3 Things to Start Doing Today for a Highly Personalized Candidate Experience


Action Why it matters Impact


Prepare candidates at every stage Candidates who feel informed can put their best foot forward; surprises in the process signal disorganization Reduces drop-off and increases offer acceptance when candidates feel respected throughout


Send clear, kind rejection messages Generic rejections, or silence, signal candidates are just a number; 37% leave negative reviews after poor experiences Keeps future applicants warm; rejected candidates are 80% more likely to reapply after a positive experience


Speed up the process Candidates are typically talking to multiple companies at once; slow pipelines lose talent to faster competitors Scheduling automation can deliver 40% less candidate drop-off and 50% faster time to onsite


### 1. Prepare Candidates at Every Stage of the Process.


The more prepared candidates feel, the more capable they are at putting their best foot forward. Before each interview, you’ll want to provide candidates with critical information, like:


-


How many interviewers they will be meeting with, who they are and how they will join the interview (i.e., on video stream, etc.)


-


How long you expect the interview to take


-


How to enter your office building as a visitor (if the interview is in-person)


-


Where to park, if your office is located in a busy area


-


What the interview will consist of (behavioral questions, a mock pitch, etc.)


### 2. Send Clear and Kind Rejection Messages.


Rejection emails are easy to forget, especially if you’re hiring at scale. From a candidate’s perspective, nothing spells “I’m just a number” clearer than a generic rejection message from an[\[email protected\]](https://www.dover.com/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#5e373038311e3d31332e3f3027703d3133) email account or the silent treatment. The best rejection messages end things on a positive note and offer to provide more specific feedback to candidates, who are often interested in learning from their interview experience with you. Wish candidates well, offer to keep in contact and, if you think they would be a good candidate for future roles, tell them that you’d like to add them to your roster.


It’s so incredibly easy to just keep up with Slack and have Dover take care of moving the candidate to the next stage. If we didn’t want to move forward with someone, they took care of sending that email, which can be really easy to forget.


**Shannon Kay, Cofounder of Prophone**


### 3. Speed It Up.


In a candidate-centered market, always assume that candidates are talking to more than two companies at a time. Recruiting comes down to volume and speed: you need to beat competitors to the punch by getting more candidates and moving them through your process efficiently.


The best way to do this is to use a scheduling automation platform that automates scheduling at every part of the interview process, including multi-step onsites. You’re also able to customize rejection and follow-up templates so that no candidate goes without communication for more than 48 hours.


## Where Candidate Experience Stands in 2026


The gap between what candidates expect and what most hiring processes deliver has widened. 61% of job seekers report being ghosted after an interview, up 9 percentage points since 2024, and only 26% say they’ve had a great candidate experience overall.


A newer pressure worth understanding:[AI screening and recruiting tools](https://www.dover.com/blog/ai-recruiting-tools-startups) and automated video interviews are now common enough that candidates have formed clear opinions about them. Greenhouse’s 2026 research found 38% of candidates have walked away from a hiring process because it included an AI interview, and among those who completed one, 51% never heard back at all. The technology isn’t the problem; the silence around it is. Teams that communicate what AI is doing, and keep a human reachable, largely avoid this drop-off.


Market conditions raise the stakes further: some estimates suggest the typical time-to-fill has climbed to around 44 days, up roughly 33% from 2021, while recruiting teams run leaner than five years ago and manage a far larger volume of applications.


### How an ATS and a Fractional Recruiter Divide the Work


An ATS gives a hiring team the structure candidates notice: scheduling links, stage-based email templates, and one pipeline showing who is still waiting on a reply. It does not source candidates, run screens, or follow up personally, so the experience still depends on how much recruiting time the team has. Founders hiring one or two roles at a time can often cover that themselves. Once several searches run in parallel, or a role is senior or specialized, response times tend to slip first.


A[fractional recruiter](https://www.dover.com/blog/what-is-a-fractional-recruiter-guide) working inside the same ATS adds that missing capacity without adding a second system. The recruiter handles sourcing and candidate communication, while the hiring team keeps real-time visibility into every stage, which can limit duplicate outreach and unanswered applicants. Where a marketplace publishes vetted, real reviews of its recruiters, teams can also assess who will represent them to candidates. Fractional recruiting typically fits companies hiring roughly 5 to 50 roles a year, and costs vary by role and recruiter.

## FAQs


### What’s the fastest way to reduce candidate drop-off without hiring a full-time recruiter?


Scheduling automation and templated communication handle the two most common drop-off points, delayed interview invites and unanswered applicants, without adding recruiting headcount. Tools like Dover’s free ATS offer scheduling links and stage-based email templates so candidates hear back at each step, and setup takes minutes with no limits on jobs or users.


### Should I use Dover’s free ATS or bring in a fractional recruiter to improve candidate experience?


A free ATS gives candidates scheduling links, rejection templates, and one pipeline view, but it does not source candidates or follow up personally. When several searches run at once, or a role is senior or specialized, response times tend to slip first. That’s where a fractional recruiter working inside the same ATS adds capacity without adding a second system.


### How do I write a rejection email that keeps candidates warm for future roles?


Lead with a genuine note of thanks, close on a positive observation about the candidate’s background, and offer to stay in touch if a future role is a stronger fit. Avoid generic info@ inboxes and silent non-responses, because candidates who receive a clear, kind rejection are 80% more likely to reapply, which directly expands your future hiring pool.


### Does using AI screening tools in hiring hurt candidate experience?


The technology itself is not the problem. Greenhouse’s 2026 research found 38% of candidates walked away precisely because an AI interview was included, but the driver was silence, not the tool. Teams that communicate what AI is doing in the process and keep a human reachable have largely avoided that drop-off.


## Final Thoughts on Candidate Experience and Hiring Outcomes


[Candidate experience](https://www.dover.com/) comes down to how a company’s process treats people at each stage, and the three areas covered here, preparation, rejection messages, and speed, are where most teams lose ground without noticing. The right fix depends on hiring volume and team structure: a company filling one role a quarter faces different gaps than one filling several at once. Dover’s free ATS pairs scheduling and templated communication with optional fractional recruiter support, which is one way to keep every stage moving without adding recruiting headcount.
